answers.question: What is the Rider-Waite Tarot Deck? What are its benefits? How can we use it?
answers.text:
The Rider-Waite deck, drawn by Pamela Colman Smith and published in 1909, is the most widely used tarot deck in English-speaking countries. Its main contribution was giving every minor arcana card a full scene. Older decks showed seven coins for the Seven of Coins. This one shows a person looking at a plant and wondering if the work paid off.

Those scenes are the benefit. A beginner can read the picture without memorizing a list, and most tarot books and courses are written around its imagery, so what you learn carries over to other decks.

To use it, start with one card a day. Write down what you see before you look up the meaning: who is in the picture, what they are doing, what the mood is. Then check a guide and compare. After a few weeks you will notice your own reading and the book's line up more often than you expected.

Any deck works if you read it consistently. Rider-Waite is a sensible first one.

answers.question: Should you turn all tarot cards right side up?
answers.text:
There is no rule, and most readers settle this by habit. Some turn every card upright before a reading, some read reversals and some never use them at all.

If you do want reversals, here is a simple way to think about it. A reversed card is the same card seen from another angle. It can mean the energy is blocked, held inward, delayed or overdone. It rarely flips the meaning into its opposite.

If you do not want reversals, turn the cards upright as you lay them out, or shuffle in a way that keeps them all one direction. Readers who skip reversals usually say the upright meanings already carry enough layers, and that fewer variables keep the reading clear.

My advice for a beginner: learn the 78 upright meanings first. Add reversals later, once you can read a spread without checking a book. Choose the method you will actually use, and keep it the same long enough to judge whether it helps.

answers.question: What does the Justice card indicate about someone's feelings and intentions in a tarot reading?
answers.text:
A single card cannot tell you what another person feels or intends. Justice describes a process: weighing facts, honest accounting and a result that matches the effort behind it.

Where it shows up in a reading, it usually points at the question of fairness. Is the situation balanced? Has everyone said what is true? Are the consequences matching the choices made? Upright, it asks for clarity and honesty. Reversed, it can point at avoidance, a one-sided story or a decision that was delayed.

If you are asking about someone's feelings, a more useful question is what you need to see clearly about the situation. Justice can answer that one. It will often suggest a direct conversation or a written list of what you know versus what you assume.

Read it as a prompt for your own judgment, and look for what the person does over several weeks. Actions answer the question the card cannot.
